questions.question: Why should `/etc/fstab` entries use `UUID=...` rather than `/dev/sdb`?
options: Device names like /dev/sdb can change between boots when disks are added or removed
questions.explanation: Kernel device names depend on detection order. A filesystem UUID (from blkid or lsblk -f) always identifies the same filesystem.

questions.question: `df -h` shows `/` at 100%, but `du` on the whole filesystem adds up to much less. Which is a likely cause?
options: du does not count hidden files
df reports in a different unit from du
A large file was deleted while a process still has it open, so its space has not been freed
questions.explanation: Deleted-but-open files still occupy space until the process closes them. sudo lsof +L1 lists them; restart or reload the process to free the space.

questions.question: What should you do right after adding a new line to `/etc/fstab`, before rebooting?
options: Test it with sudo findmnt --verify and sudo mount -a
Run mkfs again on the device
Nothing; fstab is only read at boot
questions.explanation: A broken fstab line can drop the server into emergency mode at boot. Verifying and running mount -a surfaces errors while you can still fix them.

questions.question: `df -h` shows plenty of free space, but creating new files fails with "No space left on device". What should you check next?
options: df -i, because the filesystem may have run out of inodes
questions.explanation: Each file needs an inode. Millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes while bytes remain free; df -i shows inode usage.
